I remember the sun. I remember grass, trees. I remember before the constant light, the endless grey. I remember when I could walk for hours and not see a single scrap of humanity. That was a long time ago.

A thick cloud of smog acts as an unending artificial overcast. Bright, fluorescent lights placed liberally about eradicate any trace of darkness. They burn my eyes.

Concrete and steel rule the planet. Where there isn’t a skyscraper, asphalt takes hold with an iron fist. Any plant life that pokes its way through dies quickly and is paved over.

What is most striking is the general lack. Hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of miles of road, and the only use they see are from synthetic road crews fixing cracks. The only feet the sidewalks feel are those of unknown men found rotting in the gutter. There’s always only one way in or out of all buildings. Signage is limited to a hexadecimal number stamped above each door.

This isn’t the fault of some government or corporation. This is it. This is our fault. Cultural stagnation lead to cultural atrophy. As the arts lost relevance, people began letting efficiency take over. Mechanical coldness built this world. Once the skyscrapers, or hives, went up, everybody flooded into them, and I haven’t seen anyone leave since. I don’t know if they are being compelled to say in, or if they’re just too afraid of the outside.

I remember how it started. It was determined that the most efficient way for humanity to progress was to build up, in these self-sustaining hives. Machines would take care of the people. Machines would protect the people. Machines would supply every need and want of the people. By this time, it was only natural for people to want to escape the pollution-ridden planet we had created. Hell, it was nearly impossible to breathe without some sort of protection. Soon after, machines were set up to continually, automatically make more of these hives, just in case the expanding population needed it. They soon covered the planet. When one of these massive building machines reached the ocean, they continued into it, no longer building but still moving. I cannot fathom how many of these rusted hulks still patrol the dead oceans, forever trying to fulfill their original task.

The people felt safe inside their air-conditioned, air-filtered, self-powered, self-producing bunker-tower. They didn’t need to worry about offending another person or hurting their feelings. The Machine would keep everybody happy, as long as they stayed in their air-conditioned, air-filtered, self-powered, self-producing room. Just lay down and let the Machine take away your pain, your fear, your sadness, your confusion, your hate, your dreams, your aspirations, your love.. And we, as a people, weren’t forced into this. We accepted this. We didn’t want to feel sad anymore. We didn’t want to feel scared. We only wanted what made us happy. Nobody forced us to go inside the hives and let the Machine take over. The people who entered into them knew full well what was happening, and they wanted it.

I stayed out. I didn’t want a world where I could never feel sad again, where I could never feel hate, where I could never love. I thought there would be millions who refused this fate, who wanted to live life to the fullest. There wasn’t. Every once in awhile, I see some like-minded fellow laying bloated on the sidewalk. I give him a small nod of acknowledgement, and I imagine he returns me the favor.

Even though I refused the offer of the people, choosing real life instead of chemical life, they still stole that from me. There is nothing left for me except my memories...
